question: Wildlife trafficking is not only a direct threat to biodiversity, but also a growing criminal business linked to organised crime, corruption and global health risks, as demonstrated by the pandemic. The European Union remains one of the world’s main markets for wildlife species, many of which are obtained illegally.

A recent study1 by the Commission confirms two concerning facts: a legal vacuum allows species caught illegally in third countries to enter and circulate on the European market, however, it would be legally possible to criminalise trade in wildlife of illegal origin in the EU. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission present, in this legislative term, a legislative proposal to penalise trade in illegal wildlife, based on Article 83(2) TFEU?
Why has the fight against this wildlife trafficking not been made a political priority, despite recommendations by Europol and international organisations?
Will the Commission beef up the TRACES system to cover non-CITES species and ensure real traceability?
Study on the need for, added value, and feasibility of (Lot 2) criminalising all trade in illegal wildlife across the EU.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.11.2025) The Commission agrees with the Honourable Member on the threats posed by wildlife trafficking. The study referred to by the Honourable Member assessed the need for, added value, and feasibility of criminalising all trade in illegal wildlife across the EU.

It concluded that such criminalisation is legally feasible under Article 83(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, provided it complies with criminal law principles. However, significant data and traceability gaps on species not covered by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)1 currently prevent a full assessment of its proportionality and necessity.

The study was exploratory, and no decision has been taken at this stage on a legislative proposal. Wildlife trafficking is addressed under the new Environmental Crime Directive2, which Member States must transpose by May 2026.

In parallel, fighting wildlife trafficking remains a political and enforcement priority for the Commission, which works closely with the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol)3, the EU Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust)4, and international partners.
On traceability, the Commission recognises the importance of data on wildlife trade and will continue to explore possible options to improve the current system.
1 https://cites.org/eng. 2 Directive (EU) 2024/1203 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on the protection of
the environment through criminal law and replacing Directives 2008/99/EC and 2009/123/EC. 3 https://www.europol.europa.eu/. 4 https://www.eurojust.europa.eu/.
